# Trump Trials Clearinghouse

Published on November 1, 2024

Former President Donald Trump is a defendant in a sizable number of criminal and civil cases. To help readers parse through these complex legal developments, we have centralized information on Trump’s major cases in the most comprehensive clearinghouse of its kind. Below you will find links to relevant court proceedings, key statutes, government documents, and defense documents – as well as *Just Security* resources and analysis, media and other guides.

NEW: The clearinghouse also includes *Just Security* Journalism Fellow Adam Klasfeld’s courtroom reporting and coverage of the issues. 

We will continue updating this page with new information as the trials develop. Moreover, as Trump’s co-defendants plead guilty and cases close, this page will remain a one-stop source for those matters. We hope this repository of information will be useful for analysts, researchers, investigators, journalists, educators, and the public at large. 

If you think the Trump Trials Clearinghouse is missing something important, please send recommendations for additional content by email to [email protected].

### About the Authors

#### Norman L. Eisen

Ambassador Norman Eisen (ret.) (Bluesky - LinkedIn - X) served in the White House as special counsel and special assistant to the president for ethics and government reform and as ambassador to the Czech Republic under President Barack Obama, as well as special counsel to the House Judiciary Committee from 2019–20, including for the first impeachment and trial of President Donald Trump.

#### Ryan Goodman

Ryan Goodman (X - Bluesky - LinkedIn) is co-editor-in-chief of Just Security and Anne and Joel Ehrenkranz Professor of Law at New York University School of Law. He served as Special Counsel to the General Counsel of the Department of Defense.

#### Francois Barrilleaux

Francois Barrilleaux (@FrenchwaEB) is a research assistant at State Democracy Defenders Action where he project manages amicus briefs, op-eds, and legal essays. Francois received a BA in political science with honors from the University of Pennsylvania.

Latest Update: As of July 10, 2026, two of this guide’s central storylines have moved. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that Trump’s executive order ending birthright citizenship violates the 14th Amendment, upholding automatic citizenship for children born on U.S. soil. Trump announced on July 8, 2026 that he will ask the Court for a rehearing, an outcome legal experts call a long shot since the Court hasn’t granted one in a merits case since 1965. Separately, Trump’s $10 billion IRS lawsuit, which he settled and voluntarily dismissed in May 2026 in exchange for a $1.776 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund,” was reopened by a federal judge on July 1, 2026 after 35 former federal judges challenged the settlement as collusive.

Last updated: July 2026

The Trump lawsuit story in 2026 is unlike anything in American legal history. Over 530 lawsuits were filed against the Trump administration in its first year alone. That number has kept climbing.

From states suing over immigration orders to Trump personally suing his own government for $10 billion, the legal battles touch almost every corner of American life. Tariffs, DOGE cuts, birthright citizenship, federal funding, and worker rights are all in play.

Related: Trump Voting Rights Lawsuits 2026: All Key Cases Explained

This guide breaks down every major category. Plain English. No fluff. Just the facts you need to understand what’s happening and what it means for you.

## What Is a Trump Lawsuit?

A Trump lawsuit refers to any legal action filed either against Donald Trump, against his administration’s policies, or by Trump himself against other parties. In 2025 and 2026, these cases span two very different directions.

The first direction: hundreds of lawsuits filed by states, civil rights groups, labor unions, and individuals challenging the Trump administration’s executive orders and policy actions.

The second direction: lawsuits filed by Trump personally, most notably a $10 billion suit against his own federal government over leaked tax returns.

| Type | Who Filed | What It Challenges |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Against Trump Admin | States, nonprofits, unions | Executive orders, funding cuts, deportations |
| By Trump | Trump personally | IRS leak, DOJ investigations |
| Business/historical | Private parties | Contracts, defamation, property |

Both directions involve billions of dollars and Supreme Court-level constitutional questions. Both affect ordinary Americans.

## How Many Lawsuits Against Trump Have Been Filed?

Legal analysts estimate that 20 to 30 of the 530 current lawsuits against the Trump administration are likely to reach the Supreme Court.

As of January 3, 2026, the Associated Press was tracking 358 cases, grouping them into 14 categories including immigration, DOGE cuts, and civil liberties.

President Donald Trump was facing roughly 400 lawsuits from his executive orders, far more than had been filed at the same point during his first term.

| Time Period | Lawsuits Filed | Key Categories |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First 100 days (2025) | 100+ | Immigration, funding, DOGE |
| By end of 2025 | 530+ | All policy areas |
| As of early 2026 | 600+ | Tariffs, birthright citizenship, climate |

No president in history has faced this volume of legal challenges in such a short period. That’s not a partisan opinion. It’s the documented conclusion of organizations tracking the cases across the political spectrum.

## Trump Administration Lawsuits

The Department of Justice has issued an order that permanently bars the IRS from auditing past tax returns of President Donald Trump, his family, and related companies as part of a settlement that also creates a nearly $1.8 billion fund.
The fund was designed to resolve a $10 billion lawsuit by Trump and his sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump against the IRS, citing a leak of Trump-related tax materials.

Public Safety

Public safety is job number one. The California Department of Justice is committed to advancing public safety, both in the courtroom and on the ground in California communities.

Consumer Protection and Economic Opportunity

The Attorney General's Office believes that the economic security of working families is crucial to the economic well-being of California and will fight to make sure that everyone in our state can benefit from economic growth and consumer protections.

View More

Immigration

Protecting California's immigrant communities through the vigorous enforcement of civil rights laws, consumer protections, pro-bono services for vulnerable, undocumented youth, and other programs.

Housing

Housing is a fundamental right. The Attorney General's Office is committed to advancing housing access, affordability, and equity in California
